warmup.q: static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; }. What does greeter() == greeter() print on a current JDK?
options: false: every lambda expression creates a new object
true: the lambda captures nothing, so its call site hands back one shared object
It doesn't compile: you can't compare lambdas with ==
true, but only after the JIT has compiled greeter
warmup.why: The lambda is an invokedynamic call site. The first time it runs, LambdaMetafactory links it, and for a lambda that captures nothing the linked target returns the same instance every time. It prints true from the first call, in the interpreter. A capturing lambda such as x -> x + fee gets a new object per evaluation.

sections.h: An invokedynamic call site is linked once, by library code
sections.html:
Every other invoke instruction names its target: invokestatic StackDemo.feeMinor:(JI)J calls exactly that method. invokedynamic names only a method name, a type, and a bootstrap method that will decide the target. Here is the method reference IndyTour::add in javap -c -p, and the matching entry from javap -v:

invokedynamic #15, 0   // InvokeDynamic #2:applyAsInt:()Ljava/util/function/IntBinaryOperator;

BootstrapMethods:
  2: REF_invokeStatic java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory:(...)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite;
    Method arguments:
      (II)I
      REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.add:(II)I
      (II)I

The type ()IntBinaryOperator says what this instruction does for the code around it: take nothing off the stack and push an IntBinaryOperator. How it gets one is not in your class file.

The first time the instruction runs, the JVM calls the bootstrap method with a Lookup for your class (an object that carries your class's access rights), the name, the type and the static arguments listed above. The bootstrap method returns a CallSite, an object holding a target MethodHandle of exactly that type. A method handle is a typed reference to a method that the JVM can call directly, much like a function pointer. The JVM links the instruction to it. From then on, every execution calls the target directly, and the bootstrap method never runs again for that call site.

LambdaMetafactory and StringConcatFactory both return a ConstantCallSite, whose target can never change, so the JIT can inline straight through it. MutableCallSite exists for language runtimes that need to relink later.

invokedynamic arrived in Java 7 for other JVM languages, and javac first used it for lambdas in Java 8. The design moves the strategy out of your class files and into the JDK. The bytecode says "concatenate a long and a String with this recipe". How that's done is decided by the JDK you run on, so a newer JDK can do it better without you recompiling.

try.title: Relink a call site by hand
steps: Read CallSiteDemo. It builds a MutableCallSite, calls through its dynamicInvoker(), changes the target, and calls again.
Predict the three lines it prints, then run it (or the Kotlin twin).

code.title: CallSiteDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite; /** A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. */ public class CallSiteDemo { static String eur(long minor) { return String.format("%d.%02d EUR", minor / 100, minor % 100); } static String usd(long minor) { return String.format("$%d.%02d", minor / 100, minor % 100); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); MethodType type = MethodType.methodType(String.class, long.class); MethodHandle eur = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "eur", type); MethodHandle usd = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "usd", type); MutableCallSite site = new MutableCallSite(eur); MethodHandle invoker = site.dynamicInvoker(); // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through System.out.println("linked to eur: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(362_550L)); site.setTarget(usd); // relink: same invoker, new target System.out.println("relinked to usd: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(362_550L)); ConstantCallSite fixed = new ConstantCallSite(eur); // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.setTarget(usd); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good"); } } }

alt.title: CallSiteDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite // A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. object Formats { @JvmStatic fun eur(minor: Long) = "%d.%02d EUR".format(minor / 100, minor % 100) @JvmStatic fun usd(minor: Long) = "$%d.%02d".format(minor / 100, minor % 100) } fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val type = MethodType.methodType(String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) val eur = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "eur", type) val usd = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "usd", type) val site = MutableCallSite(eur) val invoker = site.dynamicInvoker() // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through println("linked to eur: " + invoker.invoke(362_550L) as String) site.target = usd // relink: same invoker, new target println("relinked to usd: " + invoker.invoke(362_550L) as String) val fixed = ConstantCallSite(eur) // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.target = usd } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good") } }

try.expect: linked to eur: 3625.50 EUR, then relinked to usd: $3625.50 through the very same invoker, then a line saying ConstantCallSite.setTarget threw UnsupportedOperationException. An invokedynamic instruction calls through its call site the way the invoker does. Lambdas get the constant kind, linked for good.

video.title: A lambda is a body method plus an invokedynamic that LambdaMetafactory links once

sections.h: A lambda is a hidden class that LambdaMetafactory spins at first use
sections.html:
javac turns a lambda into two things: a private method holding the body, and an invokedynamic that produces the object.

Java
static IntUnaryOperator plus(int fee) { return x -> x + fee; }
Kotlin
fun plus(fee: Int): (Int) -> Int = { x -> x + fee }

javac:   invokedynamic #1:applyAsInt:(I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator;
         private static int lambda$plus$1(int, int)          // (fee, x): captures first
         bootstrap args: (I)I, lambda$plus$1:(II)I, (I)I

kotlinc: invokedynamic #1:invoke:(I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1;
         private static final int plus$lambda$0(int, int)
         bootstrap args: (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, plus$lambda$0:(II)I,
                         (Ljava/lang/Integer;)Ljava/lang/Integer;

Read the call site type as a factory: (I)IntUnaryOperator means "give me the captured int, and I'll give you an operator". The body method takes the captured values first, then the lambda's own parameters. The three static arguments are the interface method's erased type, the body, and the interface method's type as this lambda uses it. Kotlin's Function1.invoke is erased to (Object)Object, so the third argument, (Integer)Integer, tells the metafactory to insert boxing and casts.

At link time LambdaMetafactory generates a class named like IndyTour$$Lambda/0x00000007c0000a08. It's a hidden class, defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass as a nestmate of IndyTour: a class allowed to use IndyTour's private members, which is how it may call the private body. Class.forName on its name throws ClassNotFoundException. Since JDK 24 the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API from lesson 6.

The demo shows the allocation rule. A lambda that captures nothing is linked to a single shared instance, so greeter() == greeter() is true. A capturing lambda gets a new object each time the expression is evaluated, but every object shares one class. That's one small allocation per evaluation, not per call of the lambda.

Kotlin compiles lambdas the same way, which has been the default since Kotlin 2.0. The release notes list what you give up: such a lambda isn't serializable, and its toString() is less readable. Function references differ. In the demo, ::addMinor stored as (Int, Int) -> Int compiled to an ordinary generated class, IndyTourKt$main$ref$1, and isHidden is false.

try.title: Tour the lambdas
steps: Run IndyTour, then IndyTourKt. Compare the class names they print.
From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.class | grep -E 'invokedynamic|lambda' and match each invokedynamic to a line of source.
Do the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.class, and run ls on that folder. Which Kotlin construct got a class file of its own?

code.title: IndyTour.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator; import java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Lambdas, a method reference, string concatenation and a record: every one is an invokedynamic. */ public class IndyTour { record Fee(String currency, long amountMinor) {} static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; } // captures nothing static IntUnaryOperator plus(int fee) { return x -> x + fee; } // captures fee public static void main(String[] args) { IntBinaryOperator ref = IndyTour::add; Class<?> c = ref.getClass(); System.out.println("method ref: " + ref.applyAsInt(1_250, 30) + ", class " + c.getName()); System.out.println("hidden: " + c.isHidden() + ", nestmate of IndyTour: " + (c.getNestHost() == IndyTour.class)); try { Class.forName(c.getName()); } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { System.out.println("Class.forName(its name): ClassNotFoundException"); } System.out.println("captures nothing: same object both times? " + (greeter() == greeter())); IntUnaryOperator p30 = plus(30), p45 = plus(45); System.out.println("captures fee: same object? " + (p30 == p45) + ", same class? " + (p30.getClass() == p45.getClass())); Fee fee = new Fee("EUR", 3_625); System.out.println("concat: " + fee.amountMinor() + " " + fee.currency() + ", record: " + fee); } }

Kotlin: the lambdas print IndyTourKt$$Lambda/0x... and hidden: true, but the function reference prints IndyTourKt$main$ref$1 and hidden: false. It's the IndyTourKt$main$ref$1.class file in the folder. Both programs also contain several makeConcatWithConstants call sites, one per string they build.

refs.title: What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic

sections.h: String concatenation, records and switches go through bootstrap methods too
sections.html:
Since JDK 9 (JEP 280), javac compiles + on strings to one invokedynamic per expression, linked by StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. The constant parts travel as a recipe string, with \u0001 marking each argument:

Java
"concat: " + fee.amountMinor() + " " + fee.currency() + ", record: " + fee
Kotlin
"template: ${fee.amountMinor} ${fee.currency}, data class: $fee"

invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants:(JLjava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
recipe: concat: \u0001 \u0001, record: \u0001

The call site type lists the dynamic values in order. Here javac first turned the record into a String with String.valueOf, and kotlinc passed the data class object as is. Kotlin templates compile the same way when the JVM target is 9 or newer, which is what the labs use. With kotlinc's command-line default of Java 8, the same template becomes a StringBuilder chain.

Records push the idea further. A record's toString, hashCode and equals are each two instructions and an invokedynamic. The bootstrap is java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), and its static arguments describe the record:

ObjectMethods.bootstrap
  Method arguments:
    workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Fee
    currency;amountMinor
    REF_getField IndyTour$Fee.currency:Ljava/lang/String;
    REF_getField IndyTour$Fee.amountMinor:J

The JDK builds the three methods from that description at first use. A Kotlin data class takes the other road: kotlinc writes the toString body itself, getfield currency, getfield amountMinor, then a concatenation invokedynamic. Both print the same kind of text. The record carries a description, while the data class carries finished code.

Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type compiles to invokedynamic typeSwitch with java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps. javac 21 also emits the constant form, condy (CONSTANT_Dynamic), for enum case labels in such a switch. A condy entry is a constant whose value a bootstrap method computes on first use, through ConstantBootstraps. Same idea, for values instead of calls.

try.title: A record and a data class, side by side
steps: From labs/ (after running IndyTour and IndyTourKt once), run the two javap commands below.
In the record, find which bootstrap method its toString uses and the string that lists its components.
In the data class, find the recipe that toString passes to makeConcatWithConstants.

code.html: javap -v 'bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Fee.class' | grep -A6 BootstrapMethods javap -v bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/KFee.class | grep -A3 BootstrapMethods

The data class has only a StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants bootstrap, with a recipe like KFee(currency=\u0001, amountMinor=\u0001). Its hashCode and equals are plain bytecode that kotlinc wrote.

sections.h: You can call the bootstrap methods yourself
sections.html:
A bootstrap method is a public static method, so your code can call it too. That is today's lab. LambdaMetafactory.metafactory takes six arguments, and javap -v already showed you all of them:

Java
CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
        lookup,                                 // 1. caller: must be able to see the body
        "get",                                  // 2. interface method name
        methodType(Supplier.class),             // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface
        methodType(Object.class),               // 4. interface method type, erased
        lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)),  // 5. body
        methodType(String.class));              // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it
Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke();
Kotlin
val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
    lookup,                                     // 1. caller: must be able to see the body
    "get",                                      // 2. interface method name
    methodType(Supplier::class.java),           // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface
    methodType(Any::class.java),                // 4. interface method type, erased
    lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)),  // 5. body
    methodType(String::class.java),             // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it
)
val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String>

The JVM supplies arguments 1 to 3 from the call site; the static arguments are 4 to 6. getTarget() is the factory. Calling it runs what the invokedynamic instruction would run on every execution: it takes the captured values and returns a lambda object. For a non-capturing lambda, call it once and keep the result. For a capturing one, keep the factory and call it once per object, which is the shape the lab tests for. The generated class is a nestmate of the lookup's class, so the hidden class in the demo is named ByHandDemo$$Lambda.

StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(lookup, name, type, recipe) works the same way and returns a call site whose target formats the arguments.

Why do this outside a lab? You rarely need to. Code that has a Method in hand at run time, such as a serializer or a router, can turn it into an interface instance once and then call it at the speed of a lambda, instead of paying for Method.invoke on every call. Lesson 4 measures that cost against a JDK proxy.

try.title: One lambda and one concatenation, by hand
steps: Read ByHandDemo. Match each of the six metafactory arguments to the javap -v listing in section 1.
Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and read the class and call-site names it prints.

code.title: ByHandDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.CallSite; import java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory; import java.util.function.Supplier; import static java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType; /** The two bootstrap calls javac's invokedynamic would make, made by hand. */ public class ByHandDemo { static String banner() { return "settlement batch 42"; } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); // 1. () -> banner() as a Supplier<String> CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, "get", // the interface method's name methodType(Supplier.class), // factory type: captures nothing methodType(Object.class), // Supplier.get() after erasure lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), methodType(String.class)); // get() as this lambda returns it Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke(); System.out.println(s.get() + " <- " + s.getClass().getName() + ", call site: " + site.getClass().getSimpleName()); // 2. "batch " + id + " has " + count + " payments" CallSite concat = StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants( lookup, "concat", methodType(String.class, int.class, long.class), "batch \u0001 has \u0001 payments"); MethodHandle mh = concat.getTarget(); System.out.println((String) mh.invokeExact(42, 1_250L) + " <- call site: " + concat.getClass().getSimpleName()); } }

alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType import java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory import java.util.function.Supplier object Banners { @JvmStatic fun banner() = "settlement batch 42" } // The two bootstrap calls an invokedynamic would make, made by hand from Kotlin. fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() // 1. () -> banner() as a Supplier<String> val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, "get", // the interface method's name methodType(Supplier::class.java), // factory type: captures nothing methodType(Any::class.java), // Supplier.get() after erasure lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), methodType(String::class.java), // get() as this lambda returns it ) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String> println("${s.get()} <- ${s.javaClass.name}, call site: ${site.javaClass.simpleName}") // 2. "batch " + id + " has " + count + " payments" val concat = StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants( lookup, "concat", methodType(String::class.java, Int::class.javaPrimitiveType, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType), "batch \u0001 has \u0001 payments", ) println("${concat.target.invoke(42, 1_250L)} <- call site: ${concat.javaClass.simpleName}") }

try.expect: settlement batch 42 <- ...ByHandDemo$$Lambda/0x..., call site: ConstantCallSite and batch 42 has 1250 payments <- call site: ConstantCallSite. The lambda class is hidden and named after the lookup's class, exactly like a javac lambda. The Kotlin twin prints ByHandDemoKt$$Lambda.

analogy: An invokedynamic call site is a phone extension that isn't wired to anyone yet. The first time anyone dials it, the switchboard (the bootstrap method) reads the note taped to the phone, which is the static arguments, decides who should answer, and wires the extension straight to that desk. Every later call rings the desk directly, and the switchboard never hears about it again. For a lambda that captures nothing, the desk always hands back the same printed form. For one that captures, it fills in a fresh copy each time. The analogy breaks because real wiring can be redone at will; a lambda's call site is a ConstantCallSite, wired once for the life of the class.
world: In a Kafka consumer, batch.forEach(p -> ledger.post(p.id(), convert(p, rate))) creates one small Consumer per poll, capturing this and rate, and calls it once per record. That's nothing to worry about. A lambda created inside a per-record inner loop allocates per record, and only then is it worth a look. The same reading helps with framework code: Quarkus and Hibernate stack traces are full of $$Lambda frames, and those are hidden classes linked by LambdaMetafactory, not classes you can find on the class path. And if a library jar was built with an old Kotlin JVM target, its string templates are StringBuilder chains rather than invokedynamic. javap -v tells you which in five seconds.
mistake: The common mistake is guessing what a lambda costs instead of reading what it captures. People avoid lambdas in hot paths because "each lambda allocates". Then they miss the real allocation: a lambda that reads a field captures this, so it allocates on every evaluation, even though it looks like it captures nothing. The fix is to check the call site type in javap -c -p. ()Ljava/util/function/Supplier; captures nothing and is a shared instance. (LFxPoster;J)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; captures this and a long, so it's a new object each time the expression runs. Then measure (the performance track shows how) before rewriting anything.

compare.title: Lambdas and function references in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Fees.java
java.html: static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } IntBinaryOperator ref = Fees::add; // invokedynamic -> hidden Fees$$Lambda IntUnaryOperator plus30 = x -> x + 30; // invokedynamic, body in lambda$main$0 int fee = 45; IntUnaryOperator plusFee = x -> x + fee; // invokedynamic with type (I)IntUnaryOperator String line = "fee " + fee + " EUR"; // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants

kotlin.title: Fees.kt
kotlin.html: fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::add // a generated class (FeesKt$main$ref$1 style) val plus30: (Int) -> Int = { x -> x + 30 } // invokedynamic -> hidden FeesKt$$Lambda val fee = 45 val plusFee: (Int) -> Int = { x -> x + fee } // invokedynamic with type (I)Function1 val line = "fee $fee EUR" // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants (target 9+)

compare.note: Both compilers send lambdas through LambdaMetafactory, so both get hidden $$Lambda classes, shared instances when nothing is captured, and one class per lambda expression. Two real differences show up in javap. Kotlin's function types are generic interfaces (Function1<P, R>), so an (Int) -> Int boxes its Int through invoke(Object): Object, while Java's IntUnaryOperator stays primitive. And in this track's kotlinc 2.4.21 run, a function reference such as ::add assigned to a function type compiled to an ordinary generated class instead of an invokedynamic. Kotlin's inline functions such as forEach and map avoid the lambda object entirely, which Java can't do.

worked.title: What does this consumer's lambda capture?

steps.say: A settlement consumer converts each payment with an FX rate and posts it. Before reading on: does the lambda capture anything, and how often does it allocate?
steps.code: class FxPoster { private final Ledger ledger; void handle(List<Payment> batch, long rateMicros) { batch.forEach(p -> ledger.post(p.id(), p.amountMinor() * rateMicros / 1_000_000)); } }

alt.html: class KFxPoster(private val ledger: KLedger) { fun handle(batch: List<KPayment>, rateMicros: Long) { batch.forEach { p -> ledger.post(p.id, p.amountMinor * rateMicros / 1_000_000) } } }

steps.say: Ask javap. The Java call site type is the list of captured values: this (because ledger is a field, read through this) and the long rate. The body became an instance method for the same reason.

So Java allocates one Consumer per call to handle, once per batch and not once per payment, and calls it once per element. The Kotlin version compiles to no lambda at all: forEach is an inline function, so kotlinc pasted the loop into handle. Its bytecode is Iterable.iterator, hasNext, next and a direct KLedger.post. Store the same lambda in a val first and Kotlin does what Java does:
steps.code: val post: (KPayment) -> Unit = { p -> ledger.post(p.id, p.amountMinor * rateMicros / 1_000_000) } batch.forEach(post) // 3. invokedynamic #0:invoke:(LKFxPoster;J)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; // private static final kotlin.Unit handleBoxed$lambda$0(KFxPoster, long, KPayment)

alt.html: Consumer<Payment> post = p -> ledger.post(p.id(), p.amountMinor() * rateMicros / 1_000_000); batch.forEach(post); // 3. same call site as before: invokedynamic accept:(LFxPoster;J)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // Java has no inline functions, so a lambda passed to forEach is always an object

steps.say: The verdict: one small object per batch is noise next to a 120 ms ledger call, so leave the code as it is. The habit worth keeping is reading the call site type. When it starts with your class, the lambda holds this, which also keeps that object reachable for as long as the lambda lives.

lab.title: Build three lambdas and a concatenation by hand
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail with UnsupportedOperationException.

Add private static final MethodHandles.Lookup LOOKUP = MethodHandles.lookup();. Write adder() with LambdaMetafactory.metafactory: name applyAsInt, factory type ()IntBinaryOperator, both interface types (II)I, and LOOKUP.findStatic(HandMadeLambdas.class, "addMinor", ...). Invoke the factory once, store the object in a static field, and return it every time.

Write plusFee(int). The factory type is (int)IntUnaryOperator, the interface types are (I)I, and the body is addFee, whose first parameter receives the captured fee. Store the factory handle (site.getTarget()), not an object, and call (IntUnaryOperator) factory.invokeExact(feeMinor) on each call.
Write lengthOf() with LOOKUP.findVirtual(String.class, "length", methodType(int.class)). The erased type is (Object)Object, and the instantiated type is (String)Integer.
Write receipt() with StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(LOOKUP, "receipt", methodType(String.class, long.class, String.class), "paid \u0001 to \u0001") and return the call site's target.
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: Bootstrap methods throw checked exceptions. Wrap them once in a small helper that rethrows as ExceptionInInitializerError or IllegalStateException. Mind the order of your static fields: lesson 1's rule applies.

LambdaConversionException: Type mismatch usually means the instantiated type (the sixth argument) doesn't match the body's parameters after the captured ones. For plusFee the body is (int, int)int, and the lambda's own part is (int)int.
invokeExact needs the exact static type: cast the result to IntUnaryOperator and pass an int. invoke is more forgiving if you get stuck.

drill.title: Spell out a metafactory call
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write the code that turns a static method static String banner() into a Supplier<String> with LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, without a lambda or method reference. Label the six arguments. Then say which arguments the JVM supplies and which come from the BootstrapMethods table.

answer.html: MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller (JVM supplies it) "get", // 2. interface method name (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Supplier.class), // 3. factory type (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Object.class), // 4. erased interface type (static argument) lookup.findStatic(Owner.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), // 5. body (static argument) methodType(String.class)); // 6. instantiated type (static argument) @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke();

alt.html: val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller (JVM supplies it) "get", // 2. interface method name (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Supplier::class.java), // 3. factory type (JVM, from the call site) methodType(Any::class.java), // 4. erased interface type (static argument) lookup.findStatic(Owner::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), // 5. body methodType(String::class.java), // 6. instantiated type (static argument) ) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String>

recap: invokedynamic names a method name, a type and a bootstrap method. The bootstrap method runs once per call site and returns a CallSite; afterwards the instruction calls its target directly.
A lambda is a private body method plus an invokedynamic. The call site type lists the captured values, and LambdaMetafactory spins a hidden $$Lambda class at first use.
Capturing nothing gives one shared instance; capturing gives a new object per evaluation, all of one class. Reading a field captures this.

String + and Kotlin templates (JVM target 9+) use StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants with a \u0001 recipe. Records use ObjectMethods.bootstrap; pattern switches use SwitchBootstraps, and enum labels in them use condy.
Kotlin lambdas use invokedynamic by default since Kotlin 2.0, inline functions such as forEach create no lambda at all, and a function reference became a generated class in this track's run.
Bootstrap methods are public: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory takes caller, name, factory type, erased type, body and instantiated type.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate what happens, from javac to the first call, when Java code says IntUnaryOperator plus = x -> x + fee;, and why the second time the line runs is cheaper than the first.
explain.answer: javac moves the body into a private static method, lambda$...$0(int fee, int x), with the captured fee first. Where the lambda appears, it emits an invokedynamic whose type is (I)IntUnaryOperator, plus a BootstrapMethods entry pointing at LambdaMetafactory.metafactory with the erased interface type, the body and the instantiated type. The first time the line runs, the JVM calls the metafactory, which spins a hidden $$Lambda class that implements applyAsInt by calling the body, and returns a ConstantCallSite whose target constructs that class. The JVM links the instruction to it. The second time, there's no bootstrap and no class generation: the instruction calls the target, which allocates one object holding fee. If the lambda captured nothing, it would just return the same instance.

deeper.html:
Condy is easy to see. Compile this with javac 21 and run javap -v:

Java
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(int r) implements Shape {}
enum Square implements Shape { UNIT }

static String name(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c -> "circle " + c.r();
        case Square.UNIT -> "unit square";
    };
}
Kotlin
// kotlinc compiles this `when` to an instanceof check and an enum comparison: no typeSwitch
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Int) : Shape
enum class Square : Shape { UNIT }

fun name(s: Shape) = when (s) {
    is Circle -> "circle ${s.r}"
    Square.UNIT -> "unit square"
}

The switch becomes invokedynamic typeSwitch:(Ljava/lang/Object;I)I with SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. Among its static arguments is a Dynamic constant-pool entry, shown as invoke:Ljava/lang/Enum$EnumDesc;, whose own bootstrap is ConstantBootstraps.invoke applied to Enum$EnumDesc.of. The enum label is built lazily, the first time the switch needs it, instead of forcing Square to initialize when the class loads.

The lambda spinner changed tools recently. At jdk-23-ga, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory imports the JDK's internal copy of ASM; at jdk-24-ga it imports java.lang.classfile. Your class files didn't change at all. That's the point of invokedynamic: the JDK swapped its strategy underneath, and every lambda compiled since Java 8 picked it up.
